strengths: The proposed conditional routing framework (using a lightweight classifier to activate safety-tuned adapters only when necessary) is a highly practical and elegant solution to mitigate the safety-helpfulness trade-off.

The layer-wise representation probing analysis is insightful, showing that safety-related information stabilizes and becomes highly detectable from the middle layers (layer 15 out of 32 in Mistral-7B) onwards.
The paper is very well-written, easy to follow, and the motivation is clear.
weaknesses: Unfair/Biased Baseline Comparison: The 'Last Token MLP' and 'Transformer' classifiers are trained directly on the WildJailbreak (WJ) training set and evaluated on the WJ test set. In contrast, Llama-Guard is evaluated zero-shot without fine-tuning. This makes the comparison in Table 1 highly biased in favor of the proposed classifiers. To demonstrate true generalization and robustness, the trained MLP classifier should be evaluated on an out-of-distribution safety dataset (such as BeaverTails or Do-Not-Answer) without further training.

Limited Experimental Evaluation: The empirical studies are restricted to a single model architecture (Mistral-7B), a single safety dataset (WildJailbreak), and one helpfulness benchmark (MMLU-Redux). Testing on other major model families (e.g., Llama-3, Gemma-2) and additional benchmarks is necessary to validate that these findings generalize across different LLM architectures and tokenizers.

Lack of End-to-End System Evaluation: While the authors propose a two-step routing framework, they only evaluate the components individually (the LoRA interpolation in Section 3 and classifier accuracy in Section 4). The paper lacks an end-to-end evaluation showing the final overall Safety Score and MMLU Score under the fully integrated routing framework.

Incremental Novelty: Using representation probing (activation engineering) to detect unsafe prompts or guide safety features has been heavily explored in existing literature (e.g., Representation Engineering by Zou et al.). The core concept of routing to different adapters is also a well-established design pattern in LLM serving.

strengths: Demonstrates a practical two-step framework to balance safety and helpfulness, mitigating performance degradation on benign prompts by routing inputs dynamically.
Provides interesting insights into LLM representation spaces, showing that the hidden state of the final prompt token contains sufficient information to classify safety effectively.
Presents an intuitive layer-by-wise probing analysis showing where safety-related information emerges in Mistral-7B (around the 15th layer).
weaknesses: The evaluation is limited in scope, utilizing only one model (Mistral-7B), one safety dataset (WildJailbreak), and one benign dataset (MMLU-Redux). Evaluating on a wider array of models (such as Llama-3 or Qwen) and more diverse safety and conversational benign datasets is necessary to establish generalizability.

Using MMLU-Redux as the sole proxy for benign helpfulness is insufficient; multiple-choice QA benchmarks do not adequately capture the over-refusal behavior typically observed in conversational or open-ended creative writing scenarios.

The core technical idea of training a classifier on the representation of the last token to route inputs is a fairly straightforward application of existing probing and representation learning techniques, which limits the overall novelty of the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical problem: the trade-off between LLM safety alignment and general capabilities (helpfulness), proposing a conditional routing framework to mitigate it.
The analysis of safety representation localization is interesting, demonstrating that safety-related features emerge strongly starting around the middle layers (layer 15 for Mistral-7B).

The comparison between classifier architectures highlights a valuable insight: simpler classifiers (like an MLP trained on the final token representation) generalize better to benign datasets (MMLU-R) compared to more complex sequence-based Transformer classifiers, which tend to overfit.
The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and easy to read.
weaknesses: The novelty of the proposed framework is limited. Routing inputs through a safety classifier (such as Llama-Guard or input moderation APIs) to decide whether to process, block, or adapt is a widely established industry and research practice.

The practical justification of the two-step framework is weak. If the classifier detects an unsafe prompt, the standard and most cost-effective action is to block it or output a hardcoded refusal. The paper does not convincingly justify why running a full safety-adapted LLM (via LoRA) on malicious inputs is preferred over simple refusal generation, especially since no evaluation of 'safe yet helpful' generation on borderline prompts is performed.

The experimental evaluation is too narrow. The study only utilizes a single model (Mistral-7B), one safety dataset (WildJailbreak), and one general benchmark (MMLU-Redux). To validate the claims about representation-based safety detection and routing, the authors should evaluate across multiple diverse models (e.g., Llama-3, Gemma) and various safety benchmarks (e.g., BeaverTails, AdvGLUE).

The paper lacks comparisons with state-of-the-art activation steering or representation-based defense methods. For instance, comparing the proposed routing method against representation steering (such as contrastive activation addition) would strengthen the positioning of the work.

Important comparison details are missing or questionable. For example, Llama-Guard's performance on WJ-Test is reported as very low (0.56). The authors should clarify which version of Llama-Guard was evaluated and whether its prompt template was correctly configured, as this baseline seems unusually weak.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, training-free, and highly efficient moderation method (LPM) that operates on the latent space of the last token of an LLM prompt, incurring negligible computational overhead.

The core insight—that instruction-tuned models already encode safety features in their activations even when they fail to refuse a prompt in their surface output—is well-motivated and empirically demonstrated.

Comprehensive evaluation across 8 safety-oriented datasets and 7 neutral datasets shows that LPM matches or exceeds heavy, dedicated guard models (like LlamaGuard3 and WildGuard) without needing parameter fine-tuning.
The proposal of hierarchical prototypes provides an elegant, scalable way to adapt the moderator to new risk categories by simply adding new latent vectors without model retraining.
The paper is very well-written, with clear figures, comprehensive ablation studies (on distance metrics, layer depth, data scale, and covariance sharing), and robust supplementary details.
weaknesses: While called 'training-free', the method relies on a calibration/reference dataset to extract prototypes and compute the covariance matrix (specifically, the WildGuardMix training set). The dependency on this reference set's quality and domain coverage could be discussed more thoroughly.

The generalization of the latent representations under advanced jailbreaking techniques (such as prefix-injection, cipher-based prompts, or complex multi-turn scenarios) is not deeply analyzed, which could be a potential point of failure for latent-based methods.

As shown in Section 5.4, the method's performance drops on pretrained models for out-of-distribution datasets, indicating a strong dependency on the underlying instruction-tuning/safety-alignment process of the base LLM.

strengths: Insightful initial analysis showing the alignment gap: LLMs can successfully classify a prompt as unsafe when explicitly prompted, yet still produce unsafe responses if the safety check is omitted.
The proposed Latent Prototype Moderator (LPM) is elegant, lightweight, and training-free, requiring no parameter updates while leveraging existing hidden states during the forward pass.

Strong empirical results across 8 harmful and 7 neutral datasets, showing that LPM (especially with Mahalanobis distance) matches or outperforms state-of-the-art dedicated guard models (like WildGuard and LlamaGuard3).
Thorough ablation studies and robustness analyses, covering layer depth, number of calibration samples, and adaptability to emerging threat categories using hierarchical prototypes.
weaknesses: While labeled 'training-free', the method still requires a labeled reference/calibration dataset to estimate the class prototypes and the precision (inverse covariance) matrix. The sensitivity of the moderation to the choice and domain of this reference set could be more thoroughly discussed.

The moderation capability of LPM is strictly bound to the base model's internal representations. If a user wants to secure a less aligned or customized model, LPM may not perform as well compared to a dedicated, independent guard model.

The evaluation is restricted to input moderation. In real-world deployments, output moderation (evaluating the model's generated response) is equally critical, and it is unclear how well LPM generalizes to output-level safety detection.

strengths: Lightweight and training-free content moderation approach that leverages the latent representations already computed during the forward pass, resulting in negligible computational overhead.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8 harmfulness datasets and 7 neutral datasets using multiple base LLM families (Llama, Mistral, OLMo) of various sizes.
Interesting extension to hierarchical prototypes, allowing the system to scale and adapt to new, fine-grained risk categories without retraining parameters.
weaknesses: Crucial lack of clarity regarding the experimental setup in Table 1. It is not explicitly stated in Section 5 or 5.1 which training/prototype dataset was used to compute the reference prototypes and covariance matrix. If in-distribution training data was used for each respective dataset, then the comparison against zero-shot guard models (like WildGuard and LlamaGuard) is highly unfair. If a single dataset (e.g., WildGuardMix) was used as the universal prototype source, this must be explicitly clarified in the main text.

High false-positive rates on neutral datasets make the system less practical for real-world deployment. While LPM-M achieves high F1 scores on harmful data, its True Negative Rate (TNR) on benign benchmarks is concerningly low. For example, LPM-M(Mistral-7B-Inst) has an average TNR of only 90.10% across neutral datasets (flagging ~10% of safe queries) and a dismal 54.17% TNR on BigBenchHard (blocking nearly 46% of benign reasoning queries). Dedicated guard models like LlamaGuard3 consistently maintain >99.5% TNR.

The technical novelty is somewhat limited. Using Mahalanobis distance on final-layer hidden states (often on the last token) for classification or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is a very standard and well-established technique in LLM representation engineering. The paper represents a straightforward application of this concept to safety moderation.

Lack of analysis regarding sensitivity to superficial prompt variations. Since the representations are extracted from the last token of the prompt, the latent vectors can be highly sensitive to minor formatting differences (e.g., trailing whitespace, punctuation, system prompt alterations). How robust is the Mahalanobis distance to these subtle prompt modifications?
